title: Checkpoint: Growing Up and Growing Old
objective: After this level you can explain how minds change from infancy to old age and which classic findings held up.
summary: Does development come gradually or in stages, on one course or many? Culture shifts the timing, and later research revised several famous findings.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: from a baby's first bond to an older adult's look back.
cards.body: Across this chapter, minds kept changing: bonding, reasoning, reading other minds, finding words, taking risks and settling into later life. First, two questions developmental psychologists ask about all of it; then what held up and what shifted.

cards.headline: Steps or slope? One path or many?
cards.body: Developmental psychologists keep asking whether change is continuous, a gradual build on existing skills, or comes in distinct stages. Stage theories such as Piaget's and Erikson's hold that the sequence of development is the same for everyone. Culture still shifts the timing. Aché children in Paraguay, carried almost constantly while their mothers forage in the forest, walk at about 23 to 25 months, versus about 12 months in Western cultures.

items.label: Held up
points: Harlow: infant monkeys clung to the cloth mother
False belief is understood around age 5 in five cultures
Crystallized knowledge tends to hold steady with age

items.label: Revised
points: Babies grasp objects earlier than Piaget thought
The marshmallow link shrank by about two thirds with controls
Attachment is shaped by temperament and culture too

cards.headline: Chapter 7 complete
learned: How minds change from a baby's first bond to steadier emotions in later life.
Why Harlow and Ainsworth changed how psychologists think about attachment.
What later research revised in Piaget's stages and the famous marshmallow test.
When children grasp that others can hold false beliefs, across many cultures.

questions.prompt: Growing Up and Growing Old recap: what do stage theories like Piaget's and Erikson's hold about development?

options.label: Its sequence is the same for everyone
It is a smooth slope with no distinct stages
Every child follows a unique order
options.rationale: Stage theories say the order is universal.

options.label: It stops at the end of childhood
options.rationale: Erikson's stages run to late adulthood.

questions.explanation: Stage theories hold that the sequence of development is universal, even if timing varies.

questions.prompt: Growing Up and Growing Old recap: why do Aché children in Paraguay usually walk later than Western infants?

options.label: Their legs grow more slowly
options.rationale: The difference comes from child care, not growth.

options.label: They are taught to swim before they walk
Walking is forbidden until school age
options.rationale: They walk at about 23 to 25 months.

options.label: They are carried almost constantly while their mothers forage

questions.explanation: Aché mothers carry their children almost constantly in the forest, and the children walk at about 23 to 25 months.

questions.prompt: Growing Up and Growing Old recap, from Level 62: which attachment type is upset at the goodbye but happy at the reunion?

options.label: Avoidant
options.rationale: Avoidant children treat the caregiver much like a stranger.

options.label: Secure
Resistant
options.rationale: Resistant children are hard to comfort on return.

options.label: Disorganized
options.rationale: Disorganized was a fourth type described later.

questions.explanation: Securely attached children use the caregiver as a secure base, are upset at the goodbye and happy at the return.

questions.prompt: Growing Up and Growing Old recap, from Level 69: what did Carstensen's experience-sampling study find as people aged?

options.label: Everyday emotions grew more negative
Emotions stopped being measurable
options.rationale: People reported emotions at random moments each day.

options.label: Only personality changed, not emotion
options.rationale: The result held after accounting for personality.

options.label: Emotional well-being grew more positive and more stable

questions.explanation: Aging went with more positive emotional well-being and greater emotional stability.

questions.prompt: Growing Up and Growing Old recap, from Level 63: what did looking-time studies suggest about Piaget's timetable?

options.label: Babies understand objects earlier than he thought
Babies understand objects later than he thought
His stages happen in reverse order
options.rationale: The finding concerned timing, not order.

options.label: Looking time can't reveal anything about babies
options.rationale: Looking time was the key evidence.

questions.explanation: 3.5-month-olds looked longer at impossible events, suggesting they grasp hidden objects before they search for them.
